title: CSRF, Cookies and Unsafe Methods
objective: Find and fix cross-site request forgery and cookie-flag gaps on the application you own or operate locally, and prove that state-changing routes reject a request that lacks the chosen CSRF control.
whyThisMatters: Cookie-authenticated apps treat the browser as a confused deputy. SameSite, CSRF tokens, and forbidding state change on GET are different controls; this task makes you name which one you rely on and show it fail closed.
evidence: A findings note listing each state-changing route, the CSRF control used (token or SameSite=Strict, named), and cookie flags observed before and after
Git history showing cookie-flag changes and CSRF enforcement in separate commits
A committed test or scripted local request showing a missing-token or cross-site-style request rejected
A captured Set-Cookie header after login showing HttpOnly and SameSite, plus Secure or a residual-risk note for HTTP-only local labs
Reflection note answering the task questions
acceptanceCriteria: Every documented state-changing route (POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE) rejects a request that lacks the CSRF token or the equivalent SameSite=Strict cookie defense; the notes name which control is used.
Session cookies set HttpOnly and SameSite (Strict or Lax, named in the notes); Secure is set, or the notes record that the local lab is HTTP-only and name that as residual risk.
No documented GET route changes application state.
A committed test or scripted request to the local app shows a missing-token or cross-site-style request rejected.
